title: Push notification best practices for Android and iOS
description: Push notifications users keep: Android 13 permission, iOS prompts and provisional trials, App Store 4.5.4, FCM and APNs delivery, Indian examples, checks.

faq.q: Do I need to ask permission for push notifications on Android?
faq.a: Yes, on Android 13 and higher. Android's guide says notifications from a newly installed app are off by default until the user grants the POST_NOTIFICATIONS permission. The runtime permission arrived with Android 13 (API level 33).

faq.q: When is the best time to ask for notification permission?
faq.a: After the user has done something that makes notifications useful, such as placing an order or tapping an alert bell. Google suggests letting users get familiar with the app first, and Apple recommends asking in context rather than on first launch.

faq.q: What happens if a user taps don't allow?
faq.a: On Android, all your app's notification channels are blocked, as if the user turned them off in settings. On iOS, later requests don't show the prompt again. The user can only change it in system settings.

faq.q: Can I send promotional push notifications on iOS?
faq.a: Only if customers have explicitly opted in through consent language in your app's interface and you give them a way to opt out in the app. That is App Store Review Guideline 4.5.4.

faq.q: What is provisional authorisation on iOS?
faq.a: It lets an app send notifications quietly without first showing a prompt. They appear only in Notification Center, without sound or banner, with buttons to keep or turn off future notifications.

faq.q: How big can a push notification payload be?
faq.a: Firebase Cloud Messaging allows 4096 bytes for notification and data messages, or 1000 characters from the Firebase console. Apple's APNs limits a regular notification payload to 4 KB, and 5 KB for VoIP notifications.

faq.q: Do push notifications work on iPhone websites?
faq.a: Since iOS and iPadOS 16.4, web apps added to the Home Screen can request push permission, but only in response to a direct user action such as tapping a subscribe button. WebKit's announcement covers Home Screen web apps, not ordinary Safari tabs.

contentHtml:
How to get push notifications allowed and kept

In short: On Android 13 and later, and on every iPhone, push notifications are off until the user says yes. So ask at the moment a notification is obviously useful, such as after an order, not on first launch. Then send only what the user asked for, put each type in its own Android channel, and never send marketing pushes on iOS without explicit opt-in.

This guide was checked in November 2026, against Android Developers, Apple's Human Interface Guidelines and developer documentation, the App Store Review Guidelines, Firebase Cloud Messaging docs and MDN.

Push notifications are the cheapest way an app can bring a customer back. They are also the fastest way to get muted. Once a user turns off your notifications, there is no second prompt to fix it, only a trip into system settings that most people never make.

I will go through the platform rules that decide whether you can notify at all, how to ask, what to send, the delivery details your developer needs to get right, three worked examples from Indian businesses, and the mistakes that make people switch notifications off.

The platform rules, side by side

The rules differ by platform, and Android's changed with Android 13. Here is what each one says.

Push notification permission and content rules by platform

PlatformDefault for a new installWho controls when you askNotable rule
Android 13 and higherOff until the user grants POST_NOTIFICATIONSYour app, if it targets Android 13 or higherApps targeting 12L or lower get the prompt when they create a channel, usually at startup
Android 8.0 and higherEach notification belongs to a channelUser sets behaviour per channelYou can't change a channel's behaviour after creating it
iOS and iPadOSOff until the user allowsYour app, through requestAuthorizationOnly the first request shows a prompt; later requests don't
iOS, provisionalQuiet delivery to Notification CenterGranted automatically, user keeps or turns offNo sound, banner or lock screen until kept
App StoreNot applicableNot applicableMarketing pushes need explicit opt-in and an in-app opt-out (guideline 4.5.4)
Web, including iOS 16.4 Home Screen web appsOff until the user allowsMust follow a user gesture, such as tapping a buttoniOS web push works only for web apps added to the Home Screen

Source: Android notification permission and Android notification channels and Apple, Asking permission to use notifications and App Store Review Guidelines and WebKit blog, read 16 November 2026.

The common thread is that the user decides, and usually decides once. So the request is a one-shot opportunity, and the content afterwards decides whether the permission lasts.

Android 13: notifications start off

Android's notification permission guide says that if a user installs your app on a device running Android 13 or higher, your app's notifications are off by default. The app must wait until it has asked for the POST_NOTIFICATIONS permission and the user has granted it.

The user sees three choices in the dialog: allow, don't allow, or swipe it away. Swiping away changes nothing. Tapping don't allow blocks all of your app's notification channels, the same as switching them off in settings.

Two details matter for older apps. If your app still targets 12L or lower, the system shows the permission dialog the first time your app starts an activity after creating a notification channel, which is usually at startup. You lose control of timing. And Google's guide warns that for those apps, if the user taps don't allow even once, they aren't prompted again until they reinstall the app or you update it to target Android 13 or higher.

Apps that were already installed get some relief. When a user upgrades their phone to Android 13, the system pre-grants the permission to eligible existing apps, as long as the app had a notification channel and the user had not turned its notifications off. New installs get no such help.

iOS: one prompt, or a quiet trial

Apple's Asking permission to use notifications page says the first time your app makes the authorisation request, the system prompts the person and records the answer. Subsequent requests don't prompt again. Apple recommends asking in context, for example in a task app right after the person schedules their first task, rather than automatically on first launch, because people can then see what the notifications are for.

Apple also offers provisional authorisation, which I think more Indian apps should try. With it, the app is authorised automatically, but notifications arrive quietly: no sound, no banner, nothing on the lock screen, only in Notification Center's history. Each carries buttons to keep or turn off future notifications. People judge your notifications by seeing them, rather than guessing from a dialog.

Apple's Human Interface Guidelines add content rules worth pinning on the wall. Keep notifications concise. Avoid sending multiple notifications for the same thing, even if someone hasn't responded, because people may turn off all notifications from your app. Don't use a notification to show an error message; use an alert. And avoid sensitive, personal or confidential information, because you can't predict who else can see the screen.

For marketing, the App Store Review Guidelines are stricter than many owners expect. Guideline 4.5.4 says push notifications must not be required for the app to function, should not carry sensitive personal or confidential information, and should not be used for promotions or direct marketing unless customers have explicitly opted in through consent language in your app's interface, with a way to opt out in the app.

Step by step: ask for permission the right way

This is the sequence I would build into any Android or iOS app.

Step 1. Target the current Android version. Google strongly recommends targeting Android 13 or higher so your app, not the system, decides when the dialog appears. Ask your developer what the app's target SDK is.

Step 2. Don't ask on first launch. Google's guide says to let users get familiar with the app first, and gives examples of good moments: tapping an alert bell, following an account, or submitting a food delivery order. It also suggests waiting until the third or fourth launch as an alternative.

Step 3. Tie the ask to a promise. Show a short screen that says exactly what the user will get: "We'll tell you when your order is out for delivery." Google says requesting in context, so it is clear what notifications are for, makes users more likely to grant it. On Android, the explanation screen is needed only when shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() returns true.

Step 4. Consider a quiet start on iOS. Provisional authorisation lets people see your notifications before committing.

Step 5. Check before sending. On Android, call areNotificationsEnabled() before posting. On iOS, Apple says to check the authorisation status before scheduling local notifications, because people can change it at any time.

Step 6. Ask separately for marketing. Order updates and offers are different promises. On iOS, guideline 4.5.4 requires explicit opt-in for promotional pushes. I would use the same rule on Android.

Design what you send: channels and content

On Android 8.0 and higher, every notification must belong to a notification channel. Users see channels as "categories" in your app's settings and can turn each one off or change its sound. Google says to create a channel for each type of notification you send. After you create a channel you can't change its behaviour; the user has complete control.

This is useful for you, not just the user. If order updates, payment reminders and offers share one channel, a user annoyed by offers switches off everything. If they are separate, the user switches off offers and keeps the order updates that bring them back.

A sensible starting set for a business app:

  • Transactions: order confirmed, out for delivery, payment received. High value, the user expects them.
  • Reminders: appointment tomorrow, renewal due. Useful if the user set them up.
  • Messages: a reply from support or a seller.
  • Offers: sales and promotions, separate, opt-in, and the first thing users mute.

For the words themselves, Apple's guidance applies everywhere: a short title that adds context, a body that makes sense at a glance, no app name in the text because the system shows your icon, and no instructions to go and do something inside the app. Write in the language the user chose in the app. A Telugu-speaking customer reading an English notification on a lock screen is more likely to swipe it away.

For anything sensitive, such as a lab report or a loan status, send a neutral notification ("Your report is ready") and show the detail only inside the app after sign-in.

Delivery details your developer must get right

Even good notifications fail if delivery is set up badly. These are the points to check with whoever builds your app.

Message type. Firebase Cloud Messaging has two message types: notification messages, which the FCM SDK displays automatically, and data messages, which your app handles itself. The maximum payload for both is 4096 bytes, and 1000 characters when sending from the Firebase console.

Priority on Android. FCM's priority guide says normal priority is the default and may be delayed while the phone is in Doze mode. High priority is for time-sensitive, user-visible notifications; Google gives chat messages, account problems and food delivery updates as examples. But if FCM sees high priority messages that don't result in a visible notification, judged over 7 days, it may deprioritise them to normal. Don't mark silent background syncs as high priority.

Do the work quickly. The same guide says the app gets only a few seconds to process each message in onMessageReceived, enough to show a notification. Heavy work like downloading images needs extra steps, or notifications arrive late or not at all.

Priority and expiry on iOS. Apple's APNs documentation says apns-priority 10 sends immediately, 5 sends based on power considerations on the device, and 1 prioritises power and avoids waking the device. The payload is limited to 4 KB (4096 bytes). Use apns-expiration so a "sale ends at 6 pm" push is not delivered at 9 pm, and apns-collapse-id to merge repeated updates into one notification.

Clean up old tokens. Firebase's token management guide says registrations of devices that have not connected for over a month are stale, and on Android a registration inactive for 270 days is treated as expired and rejected. Sending to dead tokens wastes effort and distorts your delivery numbers.

Web push. MDN's Notifications API guide says to request permission only in response to a user gesture, and notes browsers are moving to disallow requests that are not. WebKit added web push to iOS and iPadOS 16.4 for web apps added to the Home Screen, again only after a direct user interaction such as tapping a subscribe button.

Three worked examples from Indian businesses

These are illustrative. The businesses and details are made up to show the decisions.

A restaurant or cloud kitchen ordering app

A cloud kitchen in Hyderabad launches its own ordering app. The original build asked for notification permission on the splash screen, before the customer had seen the menu.

The better flow: no prompt until the first order is placed. On the order confirmation screen, a line reads "Get updates when your food is on the way" with an allow button. Order status goes in a transactions channel at high priority, which matches Google's own food delivery example. Offers go in a separate offers channel, at most a few a week, with an in-app switch. Our page on restaurant apps covers ordering builds like this.

A diagnostic lab or clinic

A diagnostic lab wants to tell patients when reports are ready and remind them about appointments.

The permission is asked right after the patient books a test: "We'll tell you when your report is ready." The notification says only that, never the test name or result, following Apple's advice on sensitive information and guideline 4.5.4. A reminders channel carries appointment reminders the day before. Health offers, if any, are opt-in only. For larger healthcare builds, see our healthcare appointments page.

A D2C fashion brand

A D2C brand selling kurtas wants pushes for sales. This is the case most likely to go wrong.

Shipping updates are the reason to allow notifications, so the ask comes after the first purchase. Sale announcements need their own explicit opt-in on iOS, and I would do the same on Android. On iOS, provisional authorisation lets a new customer see a quiet shipping update before deciding. Sale pushes use an expiry time so a sale that has ended is never announced. The brand sends one push per sale, not a countdown of reminders, because Apple warns that repeated notifications for the same thing lead people to turn off all of them.

Mistakes that make people turn notifications off

Asking on first launch. Both Google and Apple advise against it. The user has no reason to say yes yet.

Staying on an old target SDK. The system then asks at startup for you, and a single don't allow sticks until reinstall.

One channel for everything. An annoyed user mutes the lot, including the order updates you needed.

Repeating the same message. Reminders about an abandoned cart three times a day are exactly what Apple's guidelines warn against.

Marketing without consent on iOS. Guideline 4.5.4 requires explicit opt-in and an opt-out in the app.

Private details on the lock screen. Amounts, diagnoses and loan decisions belong inside the app.

Using notifications for errors. Apple says to use an alert for an error, not a notification.

Marking everything high priority. FCM may deprioritise your messages if high priority sends don't produce visible notifications.

A monthly notification check

  • Opt-in rate for new users on Android 13+ and iOS, split by where the prompt was shown.
  • Channel by channel, how many users switched each one off.
  • Number of pushes per user per week, by channel.
  • Delivery failures and stale tokens removed.
  • Any notification that showed personal or sensitive details on the lock screen.
  • Marketing pushes sent only to users who opted in, with a working opt-out.
  • Expiry set on every time-limited offer.

Code, cloud and credentials stay in your name. Our mobile app development page has more on how we build.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to ask permission for push notifications on Android?

Yes, on Android 13 and higher. Android's guide says notifications from a newly installed app are off by default until the user grants the POST_NOTIFICATIONS permission. The runtime permission arrived with Android 13 (API level 33).

When is the best time to ask for notification permission?

After the user has done something that makes notifications useful, such as placing an order or tapping an alert bell. Google suggests letting users get familiar with the app first, and Apple recommends asking in context rather than on first launch.

What happens if a user taps don't allow?

On Android, all your app's notification channels are blocked, as if the user turned them off in settings. On iOS, later requests don't show the prompt again. The user can only change it in system settings.

Can I send promotional push notifications on iOS?

Only if customers have explicitly opted in through consent language in your app's interface and you give them a way to opt out in the app. That is App Store Review Guideline 4.5.4.

What is provisional authorisation on iOS?

It lets an app send notifications quietly without first showing a prompt. They appear only in Notification Center, without sound or banner, with buttons to keep or turn off future notifications.

How big can a push notification payload be?

Firebase Cloud Messaging allows 4096 bytes for notification and data messages, or 1000 characters from the Firebase console. Apple's APNs limits a regular notification payload to 4 KB, and 5 KB for VoIP notifications.

Do push notifications work on iPhone websites?

Since iOS and iPadOS 16.4, web apps added to the Home Screen can request push permission, but only in response to a direct user action such as tapping a subscribe button. WebKit's announcement covers Home Screen web apps, not ordinary Safari tabs.
